I see a few core problems in the industry: aggressive schedules paired with poor management. And by poor management I don't mean "shitty bosses", I mean poor strategy, poor coordination. Programmers like to have a bulletproof plan that doesn't change while they're executing it. Imagine if the blueprint for a building were constantly being modified as the building was being constructed. Floors were added or removed, kitchens were changed into meeting rooms after the plumbing had already been laid in, etc. You'd end up with a bunch of wiring, plumbing, and structural materials just jammed in places where they didn't belong and serving no purpose. The whole thing would come in way over budget, and the workers that get a boner for efficiently run plumbing lines would get angry about their work because it's impossible to do it at an artisan-level. Now on top of that add the fact that the contractor set a preposterous timeline that would be hard to meet even if the blueprint wasn't always changing. Adding more workers is just going to build more of the wrong plan before it's changed again.

"the blueprint changing" is a way to describe a thing called feature creep, where new features creep into the project requirements after work has already started. It's a really difficult problem to solve even if you're working on a one man team. When is it done if you're constantly having ideas about how it could be better? When you're not on a one-man team, the one constantly having ideas about how it could be better is (A) financially motivated to make it as good as possible and (B) is in a position of power and thus most people won't challenge the new ideas, the feature creep.

So when Team B's programming team rolls onto the A-Team's project, they don't have a clear scope of work because Team A's project manager, CTO, design director, etc keep adding features because fortnite has them or because other industry players made a shitload of money off of esports.
